newsitem.title: INDIA: Week-old India government moves to patch up split.
newsitem.headline: Week-old India government moves to patch up split.

text.p: Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's week-old government on Tuesday sought to mend a rift threatening the ruling coalition after the leader of his party refused to step down in a $280 million corruption case.
Leaders of Gujral's Janata Dal party said senior party officials were expected to meet soon, possibly on Wednesday, to try to defuse the brewing crisis stemming from the "animal fodder" scandal.

Janata Dal chief Laloo Prasad Yadav on Monday defiantly rejected a call from four left-wing parties in the governing United Front coalition to quit as chief minister of the eastern state of Bihar in the scandal over animal fodder.

"Why should I resign?" Yadav told reporters late on Monday after the Central Bureau of Investigation said it would prosecute him and 55 others in the decade-old case. "I will go to the people's court for its verdict."
The Janata Dal is the biggest component in Gujral's 15-party United Front alliance with 45 of the coalition's 178 deputies in the 545-member lower house of parliament.
The 10 billion rupee ($280 million) scandal, stretching back more than a decade but uncovered last year, involved the alleged misuse of funds for an animal welfare scheme.

Janata Dal leaders acknowledged that Yadav's refusal to resign created problems for Gujral's government, which took office on April 21 after his predecessor, former prime minister H.D. Deve Gowda, was toppled in a confidence vote in parliament.
"Naturally this causes a lot of trouble when it is brewing in the prime minister's own party," a Janata Dal leader who asked not to be identified told Reuters.
"If he refuses to step down, it will make it difficult for us to run parliament and maintain public opinion," he said.
Senior party officials might meet on Wednesday evening in New Delhi to try to persuade Yadav to step down for the good of the party and coalition, the Janata Dal leader said.

"I think Laloo needs some time to get reconciled psychologically to the inevitable. We need to administer it to him in doses," said the official, who predicted Yadav would relinquish his leadership positions within a week.
"He needs to conform to the norms of public conduct. The norm so far has been, if a person is charged, he resigns."

Last year, the president of the right-wing Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), L.K. Advani, quit his parliamentary seat after being charged in a money-laundering scandal. Earlier this month, a court cleared Advani in the case.
Several ministers resigned from former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao's government last year after being linked to the same money-laundering affair.
If Yadav refused to quit as chief minister, Gujral's cabinet would be under pressure to recommend that President Shankar Dayal Sharma dismiss the Bihar government, officials said.

The upheaval in Gujral's Janata Dal party came at a particularly sensitive time as the government intended to present the pathbreaking 1997/98 (April-March) budget to parliament during a session starting on Wednesday.
Also, former finance minister P. Chidambaram's regional Tamil Maanila Congress party was expected to announce later on Tuesday whether it would join Gujral's government.

Financial markets have been watching to see if Chidambaram's party would join the government. If it does, he likely would be asked to resume as finance minister and pilot the budget through parliament.
